The marking obligation is not intended to cover systems “performing primarily an assistive function for standard editing” or systems that do not “substantially alter[] the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof.” [Recital 133](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689#rct_133)

question: Under the amended AI Act, when may providers process special categories of personal data for bias detection?
judge_reason: The answer states both key facts (exceptional processing strictly necessary for bias detection and correction under Art. 10(2)(f)-(g), subject to safeguards) and adds only claims that the Art. 4a(1)-(2) and Recital 70 sources support, including the quoted necessity test.
baseline_judge_reason: The answer states both key facts (exceptional processing only where strictly necessary for bias detection and correction under Art. 10(2)(f)-(g), subject to safeguards) and adds safeguard conditions that do not contradict them.
answer:
Providers of high-risk AI systems may process special-category personal data only in exceptional cases, and only to the extent strictly necessary for bias detection and correction, subject to safeguards and the listed conditions. [AI Act Art. 4a(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_4a)

The Act states: “the bias detection and correction cannot be effectively fulfilled by processing other data, including synthetic or anonymised data”. [AI Act Art. 4a(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_4a) The data must also be protected by technical, security and privacy safeguards, limited to authorised access, not made accessible to other parties, and deleted once the bias is corrected or its retention period ends; the reasons for necessity must be recorded. [AI Act Art. 4a(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_4a)

Providers of other AI systems may do so exceptionally under the same conditions when the potential bias is likely to affect health or safety, harm fundamental rights, or lead to discrimination prohibited by Union law. [AI Act Art. 4a(2)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_4a)

---

- [AI Act Art. 4a(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_4a) Article 4a Processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction. © European Union, https://eur-lex.europa.eu (LicenseRef-EU-Decision-2011-833)
- [AI Act Art. 4a(2)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727#art_4a) Article 4a Processing of special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction. © European Union, https://eur-lex.europa.eu (LicenseRef-EU-Decision-2011-833)

Source versions: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) 02024R1689-20260727

baseline_answer:
Providers of high-risk AI systems may **exceptionally** process special-category personal data only to the extent **strictly necessary** to detect and correct bias under [AI Act Art. 4a(1)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32026R1744) and Art. 10(2)(f)–(g). They must also meet all these conditions:

- The task cannot be effectively done using other data, including synthetic or anonymised data.
- They apply technical limits on reuse and state-of-the-art security and privacy measures, including pseudonymisation.
- They restrict and document access, allowing only authorised people bound by confidentiality.
- They do not transmit the data to or allow access by other parties.
- They delete it once the bias is corrected or its retention period ends, whichever comes first.
- Their processing records explain why the data was strictly necessary and why other data would not work.

These requirements apply in addition to the relevant data-protection rules.

- **Log and monitor activity.** Record model inputs and outputs and, for agents, intermediate decisions, data access, and tool use to help detect threats. [AML.M0024](https://atlas.mitre.org/mitigations/AML.M0024)

question: Can attackers take advantage of ChatGPT suggesting software packages that don't actually exist? How would that work, and has anyone shown it happening in practice?

Yes. An attacker can publish a malicious package under a name ChatGPT has hallucinated; users who receive the same suggestion may install and run it, potentially allowing arbitrary code execution. [AML.CS0022](https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0022)

Researchers demonstrated the risk using the hallucinated package name `huggingface-cli`: they uploaded an empty package to PyPI to track downloads and recorded more than 30,000 downloads. [AML.CS0022](https://atlas.mitre.org/studies/AML.CS0022)

*AI-generated answer (EU AI Act Art. 50(1)). Check the cited sources.*
baseline_answer:
I’ll check primary sources for the attack mechanism and any demonstrated cases, then answer with the relevant identifiers.

Yes. The attack is called **slopsquatting**: an attacker learns which nonexistent package names an AI assistant tends to suggest, registers one on a public package registry, and puts malicious code in it. If a developer later follows the same suggestion, the package manager installs the attacker’s package. Depending on the package and how it is used, its code could run during installation or when the package is imported.

There’s a practical proof of concept involving ChatGPT’s suggestion `pip install huggingface-cli`. The real Hugging Face CLI is installed through `huggingface_hub[cli]`. Under the Colorado AI Act, deployers of high-risk AI systems must, starting **June 30, 2026**, use reasonable care to protect consumers from known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination [Colo. Rev. Stat. § 6-1-1703(1)]. Their duties include:

- **Risk management:** Adopt and regularly update a risk management policy and program to identify, document, and mitigate discrimination risks. The requirements are scaled to the deployer and its systems; an exception applies to certain small deployers [§ 6-1-1703(2), (6)].
- **Impact assessments:** Conduct one at least annually and within 90 days after an intentional, substantial system modification; retain assessments and related records for three years after final deployment [§ 6-1-1703(3)].
- **Annual review:** Review each system’s deployment at least annually to check that it is not causing algorithmic discrimination [§ 6-1-1703(3)(g)].
- **Consumer notice and explanation:** Before using the system in a consequential decision, notify the consumer and provide information about the system and decision. If the decision is adverse, explain its principal reasons and data, allow correction of incorrect personal data, and provide an appeal opportunity, with human review when technically feasible [§ 6-1-1703(4)].
- **Public statement:** Make a statement about the system’s use publicly available and periodically update it [§ 6-1-1703(5)].
- **Report discovered discrimination:** Notify the Colorado attorney general without unreasonable delay and within 90 days after discovering that the system caused algorithmic discrimination [§ 6-1-1703(7)].

The Act also permits the attorney general to request risk policies, impact assessments, and records [§ 6-1-1703(9)]. [Colorado Revised Statutes § 6-1-1703](https://law.justia.com/codes/colorado/title-6/fair-trade-and-restraint-of-trade/article-1/part-17/section-6-1-1703/)
